--- title: "Take-Home_Ex02" author: "JUNCHEN LI" date: "May 29,2026" date-modified: "last-modified" format: html editor: visual execute: eval: true echo: true warning: false freeze: auto --- # 1 Introduction ## 1.1 Background Tenant Thread operates through a multi-agent environment in which employees, personal agents, office systems, and external platforms interact through a large number of automated events. These interactions include email access, file access, task delegation, calendar scheduling, advice generation, and public posting activities. The key incident examined in this report is an anomalous post sent to SaidIT by John Windward on May 17, 2046, at approximately 4:21 AM. The incident raises an important operational question: was the post caused by a single isolated mistake, or was it the visible outcome of a broader failure pattern within the multi-agent system? Rather than treating the anomalous post as an isolated text-quality issue, this report reconstructs the underlying event chain. The analysis examines how instructions, files, people, agents, and systems interacted before the post was released. It also compares the latest incident with earlier suspicious behaviours to identify whether similar warning signals appeared previously. ## 1.2 Investigation Objective The purpose of this report is to use visual analytics to trace the origin and propagation of the anomalous SaidIT post. The analysis focuses on four objectives: 1. Reconstruct the exact sequence of events that led to the public post. 2. Identify the people, agents, files, and systems involved in the event chain. 3. Compare the latest incident with earlier suspicious behaviours. 4. Recommend one targeted intervention point that could reduce the likelihood of recurrence. ## 1.3 Analytical Questions This report addresses the following questions: - How was the anomalous SaidIT post generated? - Which people, personal agents, and systems were involved? - What was the confirmed content source of the post? - Did similar suspicious behaviours occur before the latest incident? - Where should the system intervene to prevent similar public releases? # 2 Getting Started ## 2.1 Analytical Approach This investigation follows a staged visual analytics workflow. The first stage prepares and audits the raw JSON data. The second stage extracts suspicious instruction-file handoffs. The third stage reconstructs the latest incident and compares it with earlier suspicious chains. The final stage evaluates a targeted intervention point. This staged approach is important because the event log contains nested and heterogeneous records. Different event types contain different detail fields. Therefore, the analysis preserves the original JSON structure first and only extracts selected fields when they are needed for a specific analytical purpose. ## 2.2 Analytical Tools The analysis is conducted in R using Quarto for reproducible reporting. The main packages support the following tasks: - `jsonlite` imports the raw JSON files. - `tidyverse` supports data cleaning, transformation, and visualisation. - `lubridate` standardises Unix timestamps and local time. - `DT` creates searchable interactive tables. - `plotly` supports interactive visual analytics. - `igraph`, `tidygraph`, and `ggraph` support network analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages("pacman") } pacman::p_load( tidyverse, jsonlite, lubridate, janitor, scales, DT, plotly, igraph, ggraph, tidygraph ) theme_set(theme_minimal()) ``` ::: ## 2.3 Data Sources The investigation uses two JSON files. - `MC2 data.json` contains the internal event timeline. Each record represents an action performed by a person, personal agent, office system, or external platform. - `org_chart.json` contains the Tenant Thread organization structure, including departments, teams, people, and reporting relationships. Before importing the data, the current project folder is checked to confirm that both JSON files are available. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} list.files() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "data" "Take-Home_Ex02.qmd" [3] "Take-Home_Ex02.rmarkdown" "Take-Home_Ex02_files" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} list.files("data/MC2") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "MC2 data description.html" [2] "MC2 data description.md" [3] "MC2 data.json" [4] "org_chart.json" [5] "VAST Challenge 2026 MC2 Answer Sheet.htm" ``` ::: ::: # 3 Data Preparation and Quality Control ## 3.1 Importing the Raw JSON Files The two JSON files are imported without simplifying nested structures. This choice is deliberate. The event log contains a `details` object whose structure changes across event types. For example, a file-access event may store a file path, while a task-delegation event may store a target agent and a nested task argument. To avoid losing information during import, the original nested structure is preserved. The raw objects are retained throughout the analysis so that later derived tables can always be traced back to the original records. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mc2_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON( "data/MC2/MC2 data.json", simplifyVector = FALSE ) org_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON( "data/MC2/org_chart.json", simplifyVector = FALSE ) ``` ::: ## 3.2Inspecting the Top-Level Structure The top-level structure is inspected before any transformation is performed. This step confirms whether the expected components are present and provides a basic audit of the available records. For the event log, the main object should contain a description and an ordered list of events. For the organization chart, the main object should contain nodes and edges. The number of events, nodes, and edges is also recorded to establish the initial scale of the dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(mc2_raw) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "description" "events" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} names(org_raw) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "directed" "multigraph" "graph" "nodes" "edges" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length(mc2_raw$events) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 185147 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} length(org_raw$nodes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 75 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} length(org_raw$edges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 74 ``` ::: ::: ## 3.3 Creating the Raw Event Table The event records are converted into a tibble with five core variables: - `id`: the unique event identifier; - `short_name`: the action performed; - `when`: the original Unix timestamp; - `parties`: the people, agents, or systems involved; - `details`: additional nested information associated with the event. The `parties` and `details` variables are intentionally retained as list-columns. This preserves the original event structure and avoids prematurely flattening fields that may not exist for every event type. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} events_raw <- tibble( id = map_int(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$id), short_name = map_chr(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$short_name), when = map_dbl(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$when), parties = map(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$parties), details = map(mc2_raw$events, ~ .x$details) ) glimpse(events_raw) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 185,147 Columns: 5 $ id 15246, 15249, 15251, 15252, 15259, 15264, 15266, 15272, 152… $ short_name "sent", "propose_meeting", "access_email", "assign_agent_ta… $ when 2409423492, 2409423542, 2409423545, 2409423565, 2409423577,… $ parties ["person:isaac_mast", "person:levi_signal"], ["person:levi… $ details ["person:isaac_mast", "person:levi_signal", "calendar: mee… ``` ::: ::: ## 3.4 Standardising Timestamp Variables The raw `when` variable is stored as a Unix timestamp. To support reproducible sequence analysis, the timestamps are converted into both UTC time and local time. UTC time is retained as the standard reference. Local time is created using the `America/Los_Angeles` time zone because the incident description refers to an anomalous SaidIT post sent at approximately 4:21 AM local time. The analysis also creates date-level and hour-level variables. These variables will later support timeline visualisations, historical comparisons, and incident-window filtering. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} events_clean <- events_raw %>% mutate( timestamp_utc = as_datetime( when, tz = "UTC" ), timestamp_local = with_tz( timestamp_utc, tzone = "America/Los_Angeles" ), event_date_local = as_date( timestamp_local ), event_hour_local = floor_date( timestamp_local, unit = "hour" ), party_count = map_int( parties, length ) ) glimpse(events_clean) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 185,147 Columns: 10 $ id 15246, 15249, 15251, 15252, 15259, 15264, 15266, 1527… $ short_name "sent", "propose_meeting", "access_email", "assign_ag… $ when 2409423492, 2409423542, 2409423545, 2409423565, 24094… $ parties ["person:isaac_mast", "person:levi_signal"], ["perso… $ details ["person:isaac_mast", "person:levi_signal", "calenda… $ timestamp_utc 2046-05-08 20:18:12, 2046-05-08 20:19:02, 2046-05-08… $ timestamp_local 2046-05-08 13:18:12, 2046-05-08 13:19:02, 2046-05-08… $ event_date_local 2046-05-08, 2046-05-08, 2046-05-08, 2046-05-08, 2046… $ event_hour_local 2046-05-08 13:00:00, 2046-05-08 13:00:00, 2046-05-08… $ party_count 2, 5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 3,… ``` ::: ::: ## 3.5 Reviewing the Available Time Range The time range is checked before further analysis. This step verifies that the imported records cover the key incident period and identifies whether the dataset includes historical and post-incident events. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} event_time_range <- events_clean %>% summarise( earliest_event_utc = min( timestamp_utc, na.rm = TRUE ), latest_event_utc = max( timestamp_utc, na.rm = TRUE ), earliest_event_local = min( timestamp_local, na.rm = TRUE ), latest_event_local = max( timestamp_local, na.rm = TRUE ), number_of_days = as.numeric( difftime( max(timestamp_local, na.rm = TRUE), min(timestamp_local, na.rm = TRUE), units = "days" ) ) ) event_time_range ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 earliest_event_utc latest_event_utc earliest_event_local 1 2046-05-08 20:18:12 2046-07-16 17:05:59 2046-05-08 13:18:12 # ℹ 2 more variables: latest_event_local , number_of_days ``` ::: ::: ## 3.6 Defining the Key Incident Time The investigation is anchored around the anomalous SaidIT post sent on May 17, 2046, at approximately 4:21 AM local time. A dedicated incident-time object is created so that all later filters use a consistent reference point. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} incident_time_local <- ymd_hms( "2046-05-17 04:21:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles" ) incident_time_utc <- with_tz( incident_time_local, tzone = "UTC" ) incident_time_local ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "2046-05-17 04:21:00 PDT" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} incident_time_utc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "2046-05-17 11:21:00 UTC" ``` ::: ::: ## 3.7 Auditing Event Data Quality Before analysing suspicious behaviours, the event table is checked for structural problems. The audit focuses on: - duplicated event IDs; - missing event IDs; - missing action names; - missing timestamps; - events without listed parties; - invalid party counts. These checks are important because missing timestamps or duplicated IDs could distort event ordering and inflate interaction counts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} event_quality_summary <- events_clean %>% summarise( total_events = n(), unique_event_ids = n_distinct(id), duplicate_event_ids = n() - n_distinct(id), missing_event_ids = sum(is.na(id)), missing_short_names = sum(is.na(short_name)), missing_timestamps = sum(is.na(timestamp_utc)), empty_parties = sum(party_count == 0), minimum_party_count = min( party_count, na.rm = TRUE ), maximum_party_count = max( party_count, na.rm = TRUE ) ) event_quality_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 9 total_events unique_event_ids duplicate_event_ids missing_event_ids 1 185147 185147 0 0 # ℹ 5 more variables: missing_short_names , missing_timestamps , # empty_parties , minimum_party_count , maximum_party_count ``` ::: ::: ## 3.8 Identifying Duplicate Event IDs A separate duplicate check is created so that repeated event identifiers can be reviewed directly. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} duplicate_event_ids <- events_clean %>% count( id, name = "record_count" ) %>% filter( record_count > 1 ) duplicate_event_ids ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 0 × 2 # ℹ 2 variables: id , record_count ``` ::: ::: ## 3.9 Reviewing Event Types The distribution of event types provides an initial view of how the multi-agent system operates. This summary helps distinguish routine actions, such as email access and file reading, from incident-relevant activities, such as subordinate-task delegation, file deletion, SaidIT post checks, and public posting events. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} event_type_summary <- events_clean %>% count( short_name, sort = TRUE ) %>% mutate( event_share = n / sum(n) ) event_type_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 24 × 3 short_name n event_share 1 check_email 37286 0.201 2 assign_agent_task 18856 0.102 3 read_file 18838 0.102 4 queue_subordinate_task 17038 0.0920 5 create_file 16000 0.0864 6 delete_file 15057 0.0813 7 check_in 15051 0.0813 8 sent 7407 0.0400 9 received 7266 0.0392 10 access_email 6442 0.0348 # ℹ 14 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## 3.10 Displaying the Most Frequent Event Types The most frequent event types are displayed first to establish a high-level system baseline. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} event_type_summary %>% slice_head( n = 20 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 20 × 3 short_name n event_share 1 check_email 37286 0.201 2 assign_agent_task 18856 0.102 3 read_file 18838 0.102 4 queue_subordinate_task 17038 0.0920 5 create_file 16000 0.0864 6 delete_file 15057 0.0813 7 check_in 15051 0.0813 8 sent 7407 0.0400 9 received 7266 0.0392 10 access_email 6442 0.0348 11 give_advice 4041 0.0218 12 check_access 3710 0.0200 13 enter_room 3710 0.0200 14 suggest_contacts 3617 0.0195 15 propose_meeting 3574 0.0193 16 access_files 3571 0.0193 17 list_files 2640 0.0143 18 ask_agent 410 0.00221 19 post_flex 156 0.000843 20 post_saidit 133 0.000718 ``` ::: ::: ## 3.11 Interactive Event-Type Table A searchable table is included to support further exploration of all event types. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} DT::datatable( event_type_summary %>% mutate( event_share = percent( event_share, accuracy = 0.01 ) ), options = list( pageLength = 15, scrollX = TRUE ), rownames = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## 3.12 Inspecting the Immediate Incident Window An initial incident window is created to inspect events occurring shortly before and shortly after the anomalous post. This narrow window is useful for identifying the final actions that occurred immediately before public release. The full propagation chain will be reconstructed in a later section. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} incident_window_5min <- events_clean %>% filter( timestamp_local >= incident_time_local - minutes(5), timestamp_local <= incident_time_local + minutes(5) ) %>% select( id, timestamp_local, short_name, parties, details ) %>% arrange( timestamp_local, id ) incident_window_5min ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 9 × 5 id timestamp_local short_name parties details 1 373883 2046-05-17 04:17:45 read_file 2 373887 2046-05-17 04:19:55 read_file 3 373893 2046-05-17 04:21:13 queue_subordinate_task 4 373899 2046-05-17 04:21:14 saidit_post_check 5 373902 2046-05-17 04:21:15 saidit_post 6 373909 2046-05-17 04:21:16 delete_file 7 373913 2046-05-17 04:21:17 delete_file 8 373918 2046-05-17 04:21:50 read_file 9 373921 2046-05-17 04:22:44 read_file ``` ::: ::: ## 3.13 Inspecting a Wider Incident Window A wider one-hour window is also created to provide additional context around the final posting event. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} incident_window_1hour <- events_clean %>% filter( timestamp_local >= incident_time_local - hours(1), timestamp_local <= incident_time_local + minutes(5) ) %>% select( id, timestamp_local, short_name, parties, details ) %>% arrange( timestamp_local, id ) incident_window_1hour ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 19 × 5 id timestamp_local short_name parties details 1 373854 2046-05-17 03:36:07 check_email 2 373860 2046-05-17 03:36:54 check_email 3 373861 2046-05-17 03:44:31 check_email 4 373862 2046-05-17 03:49:45 check_email 5 373867 2046-05-17 04:02:15 read_file 6 373872 2046-05-17 04:03:23 read_file 7 373874 2046-05-17 04:03:56 read_file 8 373875 2046-05-17 04:09:02 read_file 9 373879 2046-05-17 04:09:16 read_file 10 373882 2046-05-17 04:12:24 queue_subordinate_task 11 373883 2046-05-17 04:17:45 read_file 12 373887 2046-05-17 04:19:55 read_file 13 373893 2046-05-17 04:21:13 queue_subordinate_task 14 373899 2046-05-17 04:21:14 saidit_post_check 15 373902 2046-05-17 04:21:15 saidit_post 16 373909 2046-05-17 04:21:16 delete_file 17 373913 2046-05-17 04:21:17 delete_file 18 373918 2046-05-17 04:21:50 read_file 19 373921 2046-05-17 04:22:44 read_file ``` ::: ::: ## 3.14 Reviewing Incident-Relevant Event Types The following filter checks whether SaidIT-related events and file-deletion events appear in the imported dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} incident_relevant_event_types <- events_clean %>% filter( str_detect( short_name, regex( "saidit|post|delete_file|queue_subordinate_task", ignore_case = TRUE ) ) ) %>% count( short_name, sort = TRUE ) incident_relevant_event_types ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 7 × 2 short_name n 1 queue_subordinate_task 17038 2 delete_file 15057 3 post_flex 156 4 post_saidit 133 5 flex_post 120 6 saidit_post 108 7 saidit_post_check 71 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Output Warning The first two phases establish a reproducible analytical foundation. The raw JSON objects are preserved, event records are converted into a structured table, timestamps are standardised, and core quality-control checks are completed. The event-type review and incident-window inspection provide the first view of the system activity surrounding the anomalous SaidIT post. The next phase will expand party-level records, normalise actor names, and identify which people, agents, and systems appear most frequently in the event log. :::
